chapters.category: Ethiopic textual tradition • Modern English research translation
chapters.title: Chapter 66 — The Angels Who Restrain the Waters
chapters.sourceNote: Translated afresh into clear modern English from the earliest complete primary-language text responsibly available for this chapter. No extant Aramaic or Greek wording has been identified for this Noahic unit within the Parables. The complete Ethiopic (Geʽez) text in August Dillmann's 1851 critical edition, Liber Henoch Aethiopice, is the translation base for all three verses: the angels prepared to release the subterranean waters, the Lord of Spirits' command that the waters remain restrained, and Noah's departure from Enoch's presence. The contrast between preparedness for judgment and the immediate command to hold back is preserved. No unattested wording was supplied, and no modern English translation was used as the translation base.

verses.text: After this he showed me the angels of punishment who were prepared to come and release all the power of the water beneath the earth, so that it might bring judgment and destruction upon all who live and dwell upon the dry ground.
verses.study: The subterranean waters are pictured as restrained power awaiting release. Their purpose is judicial, answering the corruption described to Noah in the previous chapter.
crossReferences: Genesis 7:11 — the fountains of the great deep break open
2 Peter 3:5–6 — the ancient world is destroyed through water

verses.text: The Lord of Spirits commanded the angels who were going out not to raise their hands, but to hold back; for those angels were set over the power of the waters.
verses.study: Readiness does not authorize independent action. The angels over the waters must restrain them until the Lord's command permits release, showing judgment governed in timing as well as force.
crossReferences: Genesis 8:1–2 — God closes the fountains of the deep and restrains the waters
Job 38:8–11 — God shuts the sea behind boundaries

verses.text: Then I went away from the presence of Enoch.
verses.study: Noah's departure closes the immediate dialogue with his grandfather. He leaves carrying both the warning of released waters and the knowledge that their timing remains under divine command.
crossReferences: Genesis 6:22 — Noah acts after receiving God's warning and command
Hebrews 11:7 — warned about unseen events, Noah responds in reverent faith

explanation.heading: Chapter teaching and context
paragraphs: Chapter 66 holds destructive potential and divine restraint together. Angels of punishment are ready to release the waters beneath the earth, but readiness is not the same as permission.
The Lord of Spirits commands those angels to hold back. Flood judgment therefore does not emerge from an uncontrolled creation or impatient servants; it awaits the Lord's appointed word.
The angels are described as set over the power of the waters, continuing Chapter 60's picture of natural forces under measured heavenly administration.
Noah leaves Enoch's presence with a warning that is both severe and ordered. The coming flood is near, yet its source, servants and timing remain under divine rule.

crossReferences: Genesis 7:11 — waters released in the flood
Job 38:8–11 — the sea bounded by divine command
Hebrews 11:7 — Noah's faithful response to warning
